{{short description|British chemist (1921–2015)}}{{Infobox scientist|image=Norman_Sheppard.gif}}

'''Norman Sheppard''' FRS (16 May 1921 — 10 April 2015) was a chemist and expert on the application of vibrational spectroscopy to molecular structure, in solids, on surfaces, in solution and in the gas phase.<ref name=frs>{{Cite journal|last1=Turner|first1=James J.|last2=Chesters|first2=Michael A.|date=2018|title=Norman Sheppard. 16 May 1921—10 April 2015|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=65|pages=357–380|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2017.0043|s2cid=106196948|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Biography==

Norman Sheppard was born at 15 St Hilda Street [[Kingston upon Hull|Hull]] on 16 May 1921, son of Walter (who worked for [[Reckitt Benckiser|Reckitt & Colman]]) and Anne Clarges (née Finding).<ref name=odnb>{{Cite ODNB|doi=10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.013.109989|title=Sheppard, Norman}}</ref> After attending [[Hymers College]] from 1930 to 1940, where he developed a liking for physical chemistry, he went up to [[St Catharine's College, Cambridge]] in 1940, and graduated in 1943. He studied for his PhD under [[Gordon Sutherland]] and was awarded the higher degree in 1947.

With Sutherland's support, Sheppard was appointed visiting associate professor at [[Pennsylvania State University|Penn State]] for the year 1947–1948. The 26 year old sailed on the ''Marine Tiger'' from Southampton to New York on 30 August 1947. He had a successful year, resulting in his contributing to a paper on Raman spectra and rotational isomerism.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Szasz|first1=G J|last2=Sheppard|first2=N|last3=Rank|first3=D H|title=Spectroscopic Studies of Rotational Isomerism. I. Liquid n-Butane and the Assignment of the Normal Modes of Vibration|journal=Journal of Chemical Physics|volume=16|issue=7|page=704|date=1948|doi=10.1063/1.1746978|bibcode=1948JChPh..16..704S}}</ref>

Sheppard returned to the UK on the ''Queen Mary'' in September 1948 and re-joined Sutherland's group in the Department of Colloid Science. He later became a member of the Spectroscopic Panel of the Institute of Petroleum, and received funding over three years, sufficient to set up a research group. Sheppard was next appointed assistant director of research in spectroscopy in the university chemical laboratory, and a teaching fellow at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] in 1955. He became aware of the growing importance of [[Nuclear magnetic resonance|NMR]] and persuaded head of department [[Alexander R. Todd|Professor Todd]] to seek the funding for one of the expensive machines.

In the 1960s, when new universities were being established in the UK, former Cambridge colleague [[Alan R. Katritzky|Alan Katritzky]] moved to [[University of East Anglia|UEA]]; he soon persuaded Sheppard to do the same, to teach in physical chemistry. Sheppard set up a research group and gained a professorship. He resigned his chair in 1986.

His research contributions throughout his career, which were many and important, are described in the Royal Society's memoir.<ref name=frs/>

He was president of the Faraday Division of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]], and was elected Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 1967.

===Family===

While at Penn State, Sheppard was invited by a Cambridge friend (Don Ramsay) to spend Christmas in [[Ottawa]]. There, at a party in Ramsay's lab, he met Kay (Kathleen Margery McLean). They were married on 24 March 1949 at St Jude's, Hull, and had four children: [[Eric Sheppard|Eric]] (1950), Hugh (1953), Elaine (1956) and Andrew (1960).

Kay Sheppard died in [[Norwich]] on 5 October 2005. Norman died at [[Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital]] on 10 April 2015, of aspiration pneumonia following a stroke.<ref name=odnb/>
